title: Restore IP Addresses
prompt:
A valid IP address consists of exactly four integers separated by single dots. Each integer is between 0 and 255 (inclusive) and cannot have leading zeros (the sole exception is the integer 0 itself, written as a single "0").

Given a string `s` containing only digits, return all possible valid IP addresses that can be formed by inserting dots into `s`. You are not allowed to reorder or remove any digits.

For deterministic comparison, sort the resulting list of strings.

examples.explanation: Both are the only ways to split the digits into four valid 0-255 segments without leading zeros.

hints: An IP address always has exactly 4 segments, so you're choosing 3 places to cut s into 4 pieces — backtrack on where each cut goes.

At each step, try taking the next segment as 1, 2, or 3 digits from the current position, and only recurse if that segment is a valid IP octet (numeric value 0-255, no leading zero unless the segment is exactly "0").

Prune aggressively using length: if the remaining digits can't possibly be split into the remaining number of segments (each segment is 1-3 digits), stop that branch early. A complete IP is found only when all digits are consumed AND exactly 4 segments have been placed.

solution.approach: Backtrack by choosing the length (1, 2, or 3 digits) of each of the 4 segments in turn. At each recursive call, track the current position in s and how many segments have been placed so far. Try each candidate segment length; validate it's a legal octet (no leading zero unless the segment is literally "0", and numeric value at most 255), then recurse forward. A valid complete IP is found exactly when 4 segments have been placed and the position has reached the end of s. Bounding segment length to 1-3 and count to 4 keeps the branching factor tiny regardless of input length, so pruning on numeric validity alone is efficient enough.
solution.timeComplexity: O(1) effectively — at most 3^4 branches regardless of n, times O(n) to join each result
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) recursion depth (bounded by 4), plus output size
